3.1 — The Turret: Distance & the Detection Radius

Until now the world has been passive. Coins wait to be collected; spikes wait to be bumped into. The turret is your first adversary that decides — and before it can shoot, it has to be aware. Today you break "awareness" into smaller problems, read Unity's spatial functions, and build TurretController.cs from scratch.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I make a turret notice the player?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

The turret notices me. That is the whole feature, and "how does a turret notice me" has no answer a computer can act on.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Who is my target, and where is it?what does this part do?Read: GameObject.FindWithTag against a [SerializeField] reference, both in the quick reference, and compared in the reading below.
  2. How far away is it right now?what does this part do?Read: Vector3.Distance and sqrMagnitude — quick reference, and the trade-off table below.
  3. Is that distance inside my danger zone?what does this part do?Read: The [SerializeField] tuning knob you have used since 1.4, and the comparison operators you met in 2.2.

"Notice the player" is not something you can write. Each of these three is — and none of them is about turrets. Finding a tagged object, measuring a distance and comparing a number are ordinary tools you will reach for all year; the turret is just where they happen to combine.

The test for a finished split: could you look this part up on its own, right now, in one search? "Make the turret shoot" cannot be. "Get the distance between two objects" can.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

The reading above compares two ways to acquire the target and two ways to measure distance. Say which you picked for each, and what your choice costs you.

Read the Docs ~15 min

The three parts above each have more than one valid tool. Read both sides of each comparison before you choose — you are picking on purpose, and you will be asked to defend the pick.

Socratic: Comparing Targeting & Distance Functions

Sub-problem 1: locating the target. Two ways to get a reference to the player:

ApproachLooks likePros and cons
GameObject.FindWithTag GameObject.FindWithTag("Player") Searches the whole scene by tag. Flexible — it finds things you never wired up — but scanning every object in the scene is expensive if you do it every frame.
A [SerializeField] reference [SerializeField] private Transform playerTransform; Wired directly in the Inspector. Zero search cost, and you can see what it points at. But it needs manual wiring, and it breaks for anything that spawns at runtime.

Sub-problem 2: measuring distance. Two ways to measure how far away something is:

FunctionLooks likeWhy you would pick it
Vector3.Distance Vector3.Distance(posA, posB) The true straight-line distance. Readable, and the number means what you think it means — useful when you want to display it or compare it to a designer's tuning value.
sqrMagnitude (posB - posA).sqrMagnitude <= range * range Compares squared distances, skipping the square root entirely. Cheaper — which matters when hundreds of enemies all ask at once.
  1. If you use FindWithTag, why call it once in Start() and store the result, rather than calling it every frame in Update()?
  2. Why does the sqrMagnitude version compare against range * range instead of range? What would go wrong if you compared it to plain range?
  3. You have two turrets in this scene and one player. Which targeting approach would you choose, and what does your choice cost you?
The habit that saves you here: guard first, then read. A lookup that finds nothing does not stop your script — it hands you a null and carries on to the next line, where you then ask null for its position. Write your code so that every line below the lookup assumes the lookup succeeded, because you checked it did. Two lines at the top of a method beat an afternoon of chasing a NullReferenceException from three methods away.
Build Lab: Your Turn ~25 min

Step 1 — find your turret. The Overworld scene contains two Turret instances. Pick one and note where it is, because in 3.2 you will need to know which one you are working on. Open the Assets/Prefabs/Turret prefab and read its Inspector.

You will find that an empty Turret Controller component is already attached — the same situation as your PlayerController in Unit 1. The script exists, it is wired up, and it does absolutely nothing. Also notice a child object called SpawnPoint: that is where projectiles will leave the turret in the next lesson. Note its position.

Architectural specification for TurretController.cs:

The range knob:

  • How do you expose a "how far can this turret see" value to a level designer, while keeping the field private? What type should it be?
  • Choose a default. What makes a good default for a turret in this world — look at how big the Overworld is and how fast your player moves, then justify your number.

Acquiring the target:

  • Which component on a GameObject holds its coordinates in world space?
  • Which of the two targeting approaches from the docs did you choose? Write down why.
  • Which lifecycle method should hold the lookup so it runs exactly once?
  • What does FindWithTag return when nothing matches, and what safety check must follow it?
  • What tag does the player carry? Where can you verify that rather than assume it?

Evaluating distance every frame:

  • What guard clause should stop the rest of Update() from running when you have no target?
  • How do you measure the distance between the turret and the player? Which of the two distance methods did you choose, and what does your choice cost?
  • What condition decides the player has entered the danger zone? Be careful about which comparison operator you use — you will test the exact boundary in a moment.
  • How do you report detection to the Console so you can watch it happen with no UI at all?

Step 2 — test the boundary live. Press Play and walk slowly toward your turret, watching the Console. Find the exact point where the message starts and stops.

  • Just outside your range: the Console is quiet.
  • Just inside it: the Console reports detection, every frame.
  • Walk back out: the messages stop.

Notice that detection is not an event — it is a condition being re-evaluated every frame. Keep that in mind; it will matter when you add firing.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Break "the turret notices you" into target acquisition, distance measurement, and a selection condition
  • Say, for each of those parts, where you would look it up without asking a person
  • Explain why caching a reference in Start() beats searching every frame
  • Compare FindWithTag against a serialized reference, and say which you chose and why
  • Compare Vector3.Distance against sqrMagnitude, and explain why the squared version compares against range * range
  • Explain what FindWithTag returns when it fails, and why the null guard matters
  • Build an editor gizmo from the documentation
  • Commit and push
